stem: Which clinical feature best distinguishes the rash of meningococcal disease from many common childhood viral exanthems?

options.text: It typically starts on the head and moves to the feet
It is a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash
It produces a honey-coloured crust when vesicles burst
It appears as a slapped-cheek rash followed by a lacy pattern
It begins as a vesicular rash on the trunk and spreads to the limbs

explanation: Non-blanching petechiae or purpura are a key warning sign of meningococcal disease and suggest rash that does not fade with pressure.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward is more typical of measles.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because meningococcal disease classically causes a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, which is an important sign of invasive infection.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because honey-coloured crusting is characteristic of impetigo, not meningococcal disease.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because a slapped-cheek rash with a lacy body rash is typical of parvovirus B19 infection (fifth disease).
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because a vesicular rash beginning on the trunk and spreading is more consistent with varicella.

source.hint: Think about what happens to the color of the rash when you apply pressure with a glass.
